newsitem.title: USA: Most U.S. stock index futures end pit trade higher.
newsitem.headline: Most U.S. stock index futures end pit trade higher.

text.p: Most U.S. stock index futures started the week with moderate gains after Friday's drop, with the market debating whether U.S. interest rates are headed higher soon and by how much.
"It was pretty quiet," said a floor broker in Standard & Poor's (S&P) 500 futures of closing trade. "I just think the strength of Monday has been well known."
But nearby S&P 500s showed even more resilience Monday than some brokers had expected, especially given the gentle downslope in U.S. Treasury bond futures.
"It's a very strange situation," said a floor analyst.
"We followed bonds down in the first hour, (then) we were trading strong with them and strong without them," he added.

T-bond futures ended with tiny losses but well above session lows as traders fretted over Tuesday's Federal Open Market Committee meeting and the possibility that the policy-making arm will raise rates to preempt inflation.

Traders said price action also reflected uncertainty over how the market would react if the central bank raised rates by 25 basis points. "When we'd make new highs, you'd get sellers in there and they'd get squeezed out...climbing that 'Wall of Worry,'" the analyst said.

Several technicians said they thought June S&P 500s Friday appeared to have worked off their technically overbought condition and could be ripe for a retest of the contract high unless the Fed jolts the market with a half-point rate rise.

"I still have a good feeling that we're going to see contract highs sometime around Memorial Day," said the first broker. "I still think no matter what they (Fed) do --nothing or a quarter-point -- this market is going to go higher."
June S&P 500s, also buoyed by a strong dollar/yen, did clear a couple of minor resistance levels Monday, including May 5 and May 6 highs at 838.00 and 838.40, respectively.
But the contract stalled before challenging what the floor analyst and a broker both called serious resistance near the area of 841.35, the May 12 settlement, to 842.50.
Remarks near midday by White House chief economist Janet Yellen elicited muted response. She said the U.S. economy is unlikely to grow as fast in the next few years as it has in the last four years.

Fair value Monday based on the London Interbank Offered Rate was about 3.10 points premium, brokers said. Arbitrage buy programs required at least 3.90 point premium. Sell programs needed 2.30 points over cash or less.

June S&P 500s rose 4.00 points to 836.05, Value Lines rose 2.90 to 736.20, Nikkei 225 rallied 350.0 to 20,575.0, Midcap 400s eased 0.35 to 269.90, NYSE Composite rose 2.40 to 435.70, Russell rose 2.25 to 369.00, and NASDAQ 100 dropped 3.35 to 916.90.
